title: Untargeted serum and cerebrospinal fluid metabolomics of apparently healthy rabies virus-positive dogs in Nigeria.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Rabies remains a neglected zoonotic disease of global public health importance because of its near-universal fatality, limited reliable antemortem diagnostic options, and absence of effective treatment following the onset of clinical signs. However, metabolic alterations in dogs that are rabies-positive but show no observable clinical signs remain poorly characterized.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Samples comprising brain tissue, serum, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) were collected from 231 apparently clinically healthy dogs. Corresponding serum and CSF samples were classified as rabies (DFA)-positive, while 20 negative samples were selected for comparison.
analysis.methods: Rabies virus antigen was detected in brain tissue using the direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) test, and dogs were classified as rabies-positive or negative based on the results. Metabolites were extracted from serum and CSF using a validated sample preparation procedure for untargeted metabolomics. Metabolomic profiling was performed using comprehensive two-dimensional gas chromatography coupled with time-of-flight mass spectrometry (GC×GC-TOFMS) under optimized analytical conditions.
analysis.main_results: Rabies virus antigen was detected in 20 of 231 brain tissue samples (8.7%). After quality control, 868 serum and 300 CSF compounds were retained. Neither principal component analysis nor partial least squares discriminant analysis separated the groups in either matrix. Four serum features remained significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction: Analyte 634, glyceric acid and Analyte 706 were lower, and benzoic acid was higher, in DFA-positive dogs. Analyte 634 gave the highest discovery-set area under the curve (AUC = 0.9575). In CSF, one unannotated feature (Analyte 369) was lower in DFA-positive dogs after FDR correction. Serum Analyte 634 and CSF Analyte 369 share retention times and mass spectra and may be the same compound.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Four serum features and one CSF feature differed between apparently healthy DFA-positive and DFA-negative dogs after FDR correction. These are discovery-stage candidate features that require structural confirmation, targeted quantification and validation in an independent cohort before any diagnostic claim can be made.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings may inform the development of novel diagnostic markers for rabies virus infection in dogs, particularly in the absence of clinical signs. They also highlight the potential of metabolomics in identifying subtle biochemical changes associated with rabies virus infection.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its discovery-stage nature, as the identified features require further validation. The evidence is moderate, as the results are based on untargeted metabolomics and do not provide definitive diagnostic claims.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to identify metabolic changes in apparently healthy dogs that are rabies-positive but show no clinical signs. Using untargeted metabolomics, serum and cerebrospinal fluid samples from 231 dogs were analyzed. Rabies virus antigen was detected in 8.7% of brain tissue samples. After quality control, 868 serum and 300 CSF compounds were retained. Principal component analysis and partial least squares discriminant analysis failed to separate the groups. Four serum features and one CSF feature showed significant differences after FDR correction. These findings suggest potential metabolic biomarkers for rabies virus infection but require further validation. The study highlights the value of metabolomics in understanding the biochemical changes associated with rabies virus in asymptomatic carriers.

analysis.study_design_and_population: This study reports the first molecular characterization of rabies virus (RABV) in Eritrea using archived brain samples collected between 2001 and 2024.
analysis.methods: A total of 95 samples from domestic and wild animals were screened using one-step RT-PCR targeting the nucleoprotein (N) gene.

Using archived brain samples from domestic and wild animals collected between 2001 and 2024, the researchers performed one-step RT-PCR targeting the nucleoprotein gene. Eighteen samples tested positive, with sixteen yielding sequences suitable for phylogenetic analysis. The results showed that all Eritrean RABV sequences clustered within the Africa 1a lineage and were closely related to strains from Ethiopia and Somalia, suggesting regional connectivity and cross-border transmission. analysis.scope_and_question: This review focuses on rabies virus and rabies disease. The central question is the evaluation of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) practices following suspected rabies exposure in Türkiye, examining rabies control practices and prophylaxis data from the literature.

The review highlights the need for further investigation into factors influencing prophylaxis completion, delayed presentation, and inconsistent RIG use, as well as the importance of professional training, public health outreach, and stray animal management to improve rabies prophylaxis strategies.

title: First detection of canine distemper virus infection in varie¬gated squirrels (Sciurus variegatoides) and porcupines (Coendou mexicanus) in Costa Rica

analysis.research_question_and_background: Canine distemper virus (CDV) is a multi-host pathogen capable of infecting a wide range of domestic and wild mammals, however, reports of infection in squirrels and porcupines remain scarce.
analysis.study_design_and_population: As part of the wildlife rabies surveillance programme in Costa Rica, six wild mammals (four Sciurus variegatoides and two Coendou mexicanus) with neurological signs were evaluated to rule out rabies.
analysis.methods: All brain samples tested negative for rabies by direct immunofluorescence and RT-PCR. CDV was confirmed in two of the four squirrels and in the two porcupines by RT-PCR and sequencing.
analysis.main_results: Rapid distemper antigen tests of ocular and nasal secretions were positive in both porcupines, which were subsequently euthanised. Advanced autolysis prevented histopathological evaluation in five of the animals; however, one squirrel showed severe neutrophilic pneumonia with necrosis and haemorrhage, a moderate lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate in the pulmonary interstitium, intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies in bronchial epithelium, and a focal neutrophilic infiltrate in the midbrain.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings were consistent with CDV infection accompanied by severe systemic bacterial infection. These cases represent one of the few documented occurrences of CDV in squirrels and porcupines worldwide and the first reported in Costa Rica, underscoring the need for continued molecular surveillance to clarify lineage dynamics and spillover pathways.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the importance of molecular surveillance in understanding CDV lineage dynamics and spillover pathways, which can inform public health strategies for disease prevention and control.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report on the limitations of the study, but the findings are supported by molecular confirmation and histopathological analysis of one animal, suggesting moderate confidence in the results.

analysis.summary_en: This study reports the first detection of canine distemper virus (CDV) in variegated squirrels and porcupines in Costa Rica. Six wild mammals with neurological signs were evaluated as part of a rabies surveillance program. Brain samples tested negative for rabies, but rapid distemper antigen tests were positive in both porcupines. One squirrel showed histopathological signs consistent with CDV infection. CDV was confirmed in two squirrels and both porcupines using RT-PCR and sequencing. Phylogenetic analysis revealed distinct clusters for the Costa Rican sequences. These findings emphasize the need for molecular surveillance to understand CDV dynamics and spillover in wildlife. The study provides moderate confidence due to the limited number of animals analyzed and the presence of advanced autolysis in most specimens.
